title: Partial refund is here — refund one leg, one passenger, or one passenger on one leg
summary: REFUND scenarios are no longer all-or-nothing. A new 'Partial refund' card in the scenario editor lets you scope the refund along two combinable axes: per-leg (refund only the first, last, outbound or inbound leg of a multi-leg trip) and per-passenger (refund only the first or last passenger of a multi-pax booking). OSCAR builds the OSDM v3.8 refundSpecifications[] payload for you, adapts automatically to how your provider models fulfillments, and asserts that the provider's refund offer actually matches the requested scope. Declare REFUND_PARTIAL in your Test Framework's sales flows to switch it on.
content:
Until now, every REFUND scenario in OSCAR refunded the whole booking — fine for the basic conformance check, but far from how refunds happen in real distribution, where a customer cancels one passenger of a group or gives up the return leg while keeping the outbound. OSDM v3.8 added RefundOfferRequest.refundSpecifications[] precisely for this: a distributor can scope the requested refund to a subset of the booking via bookingPartIds (which parts) and passengerIds (which passengers). OSCAR now exercises it end-to-end.

On any REFUND scenario, the scenario detail panel gains a 'Partial refund' card with two independent switches. 'Per-leg' scopes the refund to one leg of a multi-leg trip and unfolds a leg-target selector: first, last, outbound or inbound (the latter two for return trips). 'Per-passenger' scopes the refund to a single traveller of a multi-pax booking and unfolds its own target selector (first or last passenger in booking order). The two axes combine: arm both and OSCAR requests the refund of one passenger on one leg — the intersection. The wizard warns you upfront when the scenario can't satisfy the chosen scope (a per-passenger refund needs at least 2 passengers in the linked passenger list; a per-leg refund needs a multi-leg trip), and at runtime, if the booking that actually comes back can't be carved as requested, OSCAR logs a clear WARNING and degrades to a full refund rather than failing the run on a malformed request.

A detail that matters in the field: providers don't agree on how a booking is carved into fulfillments. Paxone issues one fulfillment per passenger; Bileto and Sqills issue one per booking and put all the scoping in bookingPartIds. OSCAR's resolver detects the shape — it matches fulfillments to the chosen passenger via the fulfillment's passenger references where present, takes the authoritative leg ordering from booking.trips[].legs[] rather than guessing from array order, and walks the admission's reservation and ancillary references so the scoped parts list is complete. You pick 'refund the last leg for the last passenger'; OSCAR figures out what that means in your provider's model.

This is a conformance tool, so requesting the partial refund is only half the job — OSCAR also checks the answer. The validation suite asserts that the provider's refund offer aligns with the requested scope: the refundable amount is compared against the sum of the booking parts that were actually in scope (not the full booking price), so a provider that quietly refunds everything when asked for one leg gets flagged. The appliedOverruleCode, fee structure, and fulfillment selection assertions all run scope-aware. The resolver itself is covered by 21 dedicated unit tests spanning the Paxone-style and Bileto/Sqills-style booking shapes, multi-leg orderings, and the pax-times-leg intersection.

Partial refund follows OSCAR's framework-gating rule: your Test Framework declares what your implementation supports, and scenarios may only exercise declared capabilities. To enable the feature, open Test Config, Section 1 (Test Framework), and add REFUND_PARTIAL to your sales flows. Scenarios that arm a partial-refund axis without the framework declaring REFUND_PARTIAL display a warning chip — they still run, but the report flags the undeclared capability so certifiers see the discrepancy. Note that refundSpecifications[] is an OSDM v3.8 addition: scenarios running under OSDM v3.5 cannot express a partial scope on the wire, and OSCAR will tell you so rather than sending a v3.8 payload to a v3.5 endpoint.

No operator action is required beyond the usual image update. Existing REFUND scenarios are untouched — both axes default to off, and a scenario with no partial-refund flags behaves exactly as before.

title: Test Managers now pick exactly which reports certifiers see — per report, from the dashboard
summary: Sharing with the OSDM certification team is no longer all-or-nothing. The old company-wide toggle in API Config is gone. Instead, a Test Manager — and only a Test Manager — now decides report by report what to share, directly from the dashboard: each completed run carries a 'Share with certifiers' control and, once shared, a green 'Shared with certifiers' badge. Nothing is shared by default; certifiers see only the individual runs a Test Manager has explicitly opted in.
content:
Until now, a company's reports were exposed to the OSDM certification team through a single company-wide switch in API Config: flip it on and certifiers could see everything, flip it off and they saw nothing. That was too blunt — a Test Manager who wanted to submit one polished scenario result for certification had no way to do so without also exposing every other run their team had ever launched.

From this release, sharing is per report and the decision sits with the Test Manager alone. On the dashboard, every run that has finished (completed, failed, or cancelled) shows a small 'Share with certifiers' link. Click it and that one run becomes visible to certifiers, marked with a green 'Shared with certifiers' badge; an 'Unshare' link next to the badge revokes access just as easily. Both actions are audit-logged with the Test Manager's email and take effect immediately. Testers and other roles see the badge as read-only — they can tell what has been shared, but only a Test Manager can change it.

The company-wide 'Share test reports with certifiers' toggle has been removed from API Config entirely. Per-report sharing is now the single mechanism that decides certifier visibility: a certifier sees a run if, and only if, a Test Manager has shared that specific run. Report comparisons follow the same rule — a comparison is visible to a certifier only when both of the runs behind it have been shared.

Important for existing deployments: because the old company toggle is gone, any reports that were visible to certifiers only because that toggle happened to be ON are now private again, until a Test Manager explicitly shares them. Anything that had already been shared on an individual run stays shared. If your certifiers were relying on the blanket toggle, let your Test Managers know they now choose what to submit — which is the point: deliberate, per-report, auditable sharing rather than an all-or-nothing switch.

No operator action is required beyond the usual image update. The change is picked up automatically; hard-refresh the dashboard once it's live.

title: OSCAR's logs and dashboards now read in Europe/Paris time, not UTC
summary: Every container in OSCAR's compose stack — the app itself, Loki, Promtail, Grafana, Prometheus, Alertmanager, Watchtower, autoheal — now defaults to Europe/Paris wall-clock time. Log line timestamps, audit log entries, the 'Sent at' header on outgoing emails, and the run start/finish times shown on the dashboard all read in Paris time. Operators self-hosting elsewhere can override with a single line in .env.
content:
OSCAR's canonical deployment is hosted in France and operated by a Paris-based team, but every container in the stack was running with its image-default clock — which for the Alpine/Debian-based images is UTC. The consequence was small but persistent: log timestamps were off by an hour or two relative to the team's wall clock, audit log entries didn't match the time on the operator's laptop, and the 'Sent at' line on alert emails read in UTC.

Nothing in the storage layer was actually wrong — OSCAR has always stored timestamps as UTC ISO-8601 strings in SQLite and in artifact JSON, which is the correct architecture (storage is unambiguous, display is localised). The mismatch was on the display side: the processes themselves were generating log lines and rendering email bodies in UTC instead of Paris time.

From v1.11.6, every container in the compose stack reads its TZ from an OSCAR_TZ environment variable in .env, defaulting to Europe/Paris. That's eight containers: the OSCAR app, the autoheal sidecar, Watchtower, plus when the metrics overlay is up, Loki, Promtail, Grafana, Prometheus, and Alertmanager. Two of those — autoheal and Watchtower — were previously hardcoded to UTC and have been flipped.

If you self-host OSCAR somewhere other than continental Europe, set OSCAR_TZ in OSCAR_Deploy/.env to any IANA timezone name — America/New_York, Asia/Tokyo, Australia/Sydney, etc. — and re-up the stack. The change is in the compose YAML, not in the published Docker image, so Watchtower won't auto-pick it up; operators need to git pull the deployment repo and run docker compose up -d once.

Storage stays UTC. Comparing two runs that started at different times will continue to give the same numerical delta regardless of where you're viewing from. Only the wall-clock the processes see — and therefore the prefix on every Pino / Loki / Alertmanager log line — changes. The Grafana dashboards additionally default to 'browser' timezone now, so each viewer sees timestamps in their own local time without further config.

title: Fixed: "Could not parse data file: Unexpected token 'O', OSCAR1..." when re-running a test config
summary: A regression slipped past the v1.11.0 at-rest encryption rollout: three file-reader code paths were still reading the encrypted bytes of a data file or a Bruno results artifact directly into JSON.parse, so they choked on the OSCAR1 magic header. A Paxone tester hit it after the first run worked, the test config was saved, and the second run came back with 'Could not parse data file: Unexpected token O, "OSCAR1b8mF"... is not valid JSON'. All three sites now go through the OSCAR1-aware decrypt helper.
content:
v1.11.0 introduced at-rest encryption for vendor-sensitive content on disk: company data files, JSON results, HTML reports. Every write now goes through a helper that wraps the bytes in an AES-256-GCM envelope marked with a six-byte OSCAR1 magic header. Every read was supposed to go through a matching helper that detects the magic header, decrypts on the fly, and transparently passes legacy plaintext files through unchanged.

Three code paths were missed. They read the encrypted file directly with fs.readFileSync and handed the raw ciphertext to JSON.parse, which choked on the very first byte — the capital O of OSCAR1.

The Paxone tester hit the most visible of the three: the parallel-mode datafile loader on the run endpoint. The symptom was 'Could not parse data file: Unexpected token O, "OSCAR1b8mF"... is not valid JSON' on the second attempt to start a run for a saved test config. It explains why a first run could succeed (Bruno's loopback fetch of /data is served through a different code path that already went through the at-rest helper) while the second failed (the parallel scheduler reloads the datafile from disk itself, through the path that didn't).

The other two were less visible but had the same shape: the diff engine that powers the compare-two-runs feature on the dashboard, and the structured-results parser that powers per-run report rendering. Both read .bru_results.json directly. Both would have started failing for any run launched after a company upgraded to v1.11.0.

All three sites are now fixed in v1.11.5. They use the same decryptFromFile helper used everywhere else in the codebase, which transparently handles both new (OSCAR1-encrypted) and legacy (pre-v1.11.0 plaintext) files. No data migration. No operator action — Watchtower picks up the new image automatically.

If you saw this error after upgrading to v1.11.0, v1.11.1, v1.11.2, v1.11.3, or v1.11.4, the upgrade to v1.11.5 fixes it. The underlying data is unchanged on disk; only the read side was broken.

title: Dashboard now shows who ran each test, and Test Managers can delete their company's runs permanently
summary: Two small but useful dashboard improvements for Test Managers, following the access-control restructure that landed earlier in the week. Each run now shows the submitter's email under its label so Test Managers can see at a glance which of their testers kicked off each run. And since administrators no longer read vendor test data, Test Managers — the data owners for their company — now have the power to permanently delete their own runs directly, instead of routing the request to an administrator who can't see what they're approving.
content:
The recent vendor-data-sovereignty release (v1.10.0 in particular) made one thing explicit: administrators on the platform no longer see your test data. Their role is operations and security only. That cleanup left two small bits of follow-up work in the dashboard, both addressed in this release.

First, the submitter is now visible. When a Test Manager opens their dashboard and sees a list of runs from their team, each row now carries a small subtitle: 👤 followed by the email address of the tester who actually started the run. Before, you had to click into a run to find this out. Now it's visible at a glance, which matters when triaging a batch of failures or deciding which runs to review or delete. Testers, who by definition only see their own runs, don't get this subtitle (it would be the same email on every row).

Second, the deletion flow is finally consistent with the new trust model. Until today, when a Test Manager clicked Delete on a selection of runs, the modal said the runs would be queued for administrator review and only an administrator could permanently delete them. With administrators no longer reading test data, that flow had become circular — administrators were being asked to approve the deletion of content they cannot see. As of today, when a Test Manager confirms a deletion, the runs are permanently deleted then and there. The modal now shows a clear yellow warning, the title reads Permanently Delete Runs, and the confirm button reads Permanently Delete. There is no recovery path after confirming, so the language is direct about that. Testers continue to use the soft-delete flow — their deletions still go into a pending queue that their Test Manager can confirm or restore — so the safety net for accidental clicks is preserved for the role that's most likely to need it.

No operator action required. The change is picked up automatically on the next page reload.

title: Phase 3 of vendor data sovereignty — the operational policy is now written down
summary: OSCAR's security story is now complete end to end. Phase 1 restructured who in the application can see what. Phase 2 encrypted everything sensitive on disk. Phase 3, today, documents the operational policy that closes the gap software cannot enforce alone — who has root SSH access to production, how the four long-lived secrets are rotated, how backups are protected, and exactly what to do when something breaks.
content:
Code can take responsibility for the application boundary and the on-disk boundary. It cannot take responsibility for the human boundary. A person with root SSH on the production server can attach a debugger to the running OSCAR process and read the encryption key out of memory; no software defence stops that. The only thing that does is policy — keeping the population of those humans small, accountable, and audited.

Today's release ships that policy as a written document: Documentation/Server_Operations/OSCAR - Security Operations Policy.md. It is intentionally specific rather than vague, because policies that don't fit on a single page never get followed.

The document defines three operator tiers with strictly different powers: Tier A platform operators with root SSH (limited to exactly two named individuals, public-key only, every sudo audited), Tier B OSCAR administrators (web UI only, no test data access since Phase 1), and Tier C UIC certification reviewers (sees only what test managers have shared). A person holding Tier A access must not also hold Tier B or C on the same identity, so a compromise of one credential does not cascade to the others.

It inventories the four long-lived secrets — ENCRYPTION_KEY, JWT_SECRET, PLATFORM_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN, the Brevo SMTP key — with concrete rotation procedures for each, separately tagged by impact. The ENCRYPTION_KEY in particular gets a careful section because rotating it requires a full re-encryption pass and a maintenance window. The document is clear that this key never gets rotated except on a genuine suspected leak.

Backups are now defined as daily snapshots with 14-day rolling retention plus quarterly cold archives moved to UIC fileshare for a 4-year audit horizon, with the rolling tarballs themselves GPG-encrypted using a passphrase held alongside the database key.

The incident response section is the part that took the longest to draft, because we exercised it for real this morning. A schema migration bug crashed OSCAR's production deployment for about an hour and a half. The full timeline is captured as a worked example: what worked (the healthcheck plus autoheal correctly identified the unhealthy container, Loki captured the stack trace for diagnosis, the manual schema-version bump turned out to be a clean recovery mechanism precisely because the migration was designed as a one-time backfill); what didn't (no second rollback image was pre-pulled on the host, so the only fallback was a months-stale tag); and four concrete follow-up items including pre-pulling the last three stable image tags and adding a migration integration test that seeds rows and asserts data integrity. Those four items are now tracked.

Nothing changes on the server itself. Phase 3 is documentation — the agreed rules of operation, written down where current and future Tier A operators can find them. Combined with the code changes that landed in Phase 1 (v1.10.0) and Phase 2 (v1.11.0 + v1.11.1 hotfix), this completes issue #60. Vendor data sovereignty, end to end.

title: Phase 2 of vendor data sovereignty — your data is now encrypted on disk too
summary: After this release, every byte of vendor-sensitive content on the OSCAR server's disk is AES-256-GCM ciphertext: HTML reports, JSON results, company data files, log lines, HTTP request and response bodies, scenarios, test framework configurations. A sysadmin running cat on the database file or on an artifact file sees only encryption envelopes — never plaintext. Plaintext exists only inside the OSCAR process while it's running.
content:
Last week's release (v1.10.0) restructured the trust model at the application level — administrators stopped reading vendor test data, certifiers started seeing only the runs vendors explicitly chose to share, and an anonymous-artifact-download bypass was closed. Today's release closes the remaining gap: data on disk is now encrypted at rest.

Until now, although OSCAR's database and artifact files lived under restrictive filesystem permissions, the bytes themselves were plaintext. A sysadmin with sudo access on the production server could open /opt/OSCAR/.../data/oscar.db with a SQLite client and read every log line, every HTTP request and response body, every test scenario; they could cat any HTML report from /opt/OSCAR/.../data/artifacts/ and see the full vendor results page; they could open a company's uploaded data file directly. None of that survives the application-layer access controls — it's a separate disk-layer attack surface.

v1.11.0 closes it. The same AES-256-GCM envelope OSCAR has always used to encrypt OAuth tokens and credentials at rest is now applied to the content of every sensitive column and to every artifact and data file written to disk. The encryption uses your existing ENCRYPTION_KEY environment variable — no new key to manage. Each value gets a fresh random IV and an authenticated tag, so identical plaintext produces different ciphertext and any tampering is detected at decrypt time. Files on disk start with a six-byte OSCAR1 magic header; database column values start with an enc:v1: prefix. Anyone reading the raw bytes sees those markers followed by base64 ciphertext and nothing else.

What's encrypted: HTML report files, JSON results files, company data files, log line content (run_events.message), the four HTTP traffic columns on every request row (request_body, request_headers, response_body, response_headers), the per-call context column, the test framework JSON, the test resources JSON. What's NOT encrypted: structural metadata used for queries — status, timestamps, http_method, http_status, suite names, company IDs. These need to remain searchable and sortable in SQL, and they don't carry vendor secrets.

The transition is fully backward-compatible. Files written before v1.11.0 stay plaintext on disk; the read helpers detect the absence of the OSCAR1 magic header and pass them through unchanged. Database rows without the enc:v1: prefix are treated the same way. New writes are always encrypted. A v19 schema migration runs automatically on first boot and re-encrypts existing plaintext rows — idempotent, per-table transaction, takes seconds even on large databases. Existing artifact and data files on disk stay plaintext until they're naturally re-written by a new run; an optional bulk-encrypt operator script (encrypt-existing-artifacts.sh) is provided for those who want every file on disk to be ciphertext immediately.

What this still doesn't defend against: a sysadmin with root SSH who attaches a debugger to the running OSCAR process can extract the ENCRYPTION_KEY from process memory and decrypt anything. That's a fundamental limit of any application-layer encryption — software gets you to the trust boundary; beyond that, only operational policy (who has root, audit of sudo usage, key management) provides protection. Phase 3 of issue #60 will document the operational policy that closes the remaining gap. Code-level defenses are now where they need to be.

title: Your test data is now strictly yours — until you choose to share specific reports with UIC certifiers
summary: OSCAR's trust model has been restructured. Test configuration, data files, and run reports are visible only to your company's testers and test managers. Administrators on the platform no longer see your test data — their role is operations and security only. Certifiers see only the specific runs your test manager has explicitly chosen to share, run by run. A legacy hole that let anonymous users download artifacts knowing only the run UUID is closed.
content:
This release is the first phase of issue #60, which asked for stricter guarantees about who can see what. Three things change at once.

First, the platform administrator role no longer reads test data. Until now, the administrator role doubled as a super-tester — admins could browse every company's runs, reports, test configurations, and data files for support purposes. The trade-off was that a vendor had to trust UIC's administrator team with the full content of their conformance work. Going forward the administrator role is operations and security only: managing users, managing companies (their metadata, not their test work), configuring the server, configuring alerts, viewing the audit log, accessing the observability dashboards. When an administrator opens what used to be the All Reports tab, they now see only the data-lifecycle queue (runs that testers have asked to be permanently deleted, and runs the administrator has flagged for review) — they can confirm or restore those runs without ever seeing their content. Aggregate counts (runs per day, runs per status, top submitters) remain available on the Server Activity tab.

Second, sharing with certifiers becomes a per-run decision. Previously each company had a single Share with Certifiers checkbox in its profile; once turned on, certifiers saw every run from that company. Now there is a Share with certifiers button on every individual run-detail page, visible to test managers only. Test managers pick which specific reports become certifier-visible, run by run. Each share and each revoke is audit-logged. The legacy company-wide checkbox remains in the UI as a master kill switch — flipping it off overrides every per-run share, letting a vendor revoke all certifier access in one click. A migration runs once on rollover to backfill every existing terminal run of currently-shared companies as Shared, so certifiers don't suddenly lose access to reports they had been actively reviewing.

Third, a real security hole is closed. The /artifacts/<runId>/<filename> path was previously served as static files with no authentication — anyone able to reach OSCAR (or who saw a run UUID in a screenshot, an email thread, or a browser history) could download the HTML report or JSON results without logging in. The same was true for /data/<filename>, which serves company data files to the Bruno subprocess. Both paths now require an authenticated session matching the run's owning company. Bruno's loopback fetch of /data continues to work via a narrow exception for true-localhost requests with no X-Forwarded-For header.

None of this protects against an operating-system administrator with root SSH access on the production VPS reading the SQLite database directly — the test data on disk is still in plaintext (only the OAuth credentials and tokens are encrypted column-by-column). Closing that gap requires at-rest database encryption, which lands as a separate release in Phase 2. For Phase 1, the trust boundary at the application level is now where it should be: vendor data stays inside the vendor's company, until the vendor's test manager makes an explicit decision otherwise.

title: Alerting and SMTP — one place, one source of truth, no more VPS edits
summary: The administrator panel now manages alerting end-to-end. SMTP credentials are configured once and used by everything (password reset, account verification, alerts to admins). A new Alerting card lets admins set the recipient list and re-page intervals, then ship the new configuration to the live Alertmanager with a single click — no SSH, no YAML editing on the VPS.
content:
Until this release, OSCAR had a small but persistent split-brain when it came to email. The administrator's Server Config tab managed the SMTP credentials used by OSCAR itself (password resets, account verification, test emails) — but the alerting layer that emails administrators when something goes wrong with the platform kept its own copy of those same SMTP credentials in a YAML file on the VPS. Two places, two ways to get them out of sync, one of which required SSH access to update. With this release that's collapsed back into one.

The Server Config tab gains a new Alerting card with three fields: a recipient list (comma- or newline-separated administrator emails who should receive alert emails), and two re-page intervals controlling how often Alertmanager re-emails an unresolved critical or warning alert (defaults: every hour for criticals, every four hours for warnings). Below the fields, a single button — Apply alerting config to Alertmanager — does everything else: it generates a fresh alertmanager.yml from your current SMTP credentials and the values you just saved, writes it to a shared docker volume that the Alertmanager container reads from, and triggers Alertmanager to reload its configuration on the spot. No SSH, no VPS edits, no docker exec, no YAML editing. The button surfaces the verbatim outcome inline (file written, reload status, response body) so any partial failure is immediately self-diagnosable.

While we were in the SMTP fields, two small but high-value polish changes also landed. First, the field labels were rewritten to make the difference between authentication and presentation explicit — what used to be 'SMTP User' is now 'SMTP Login', with help text explaining that this is the relay-internal authentication identity (often something like a731f1001@smtp-brevo.com) and not what recipients see in their inbox. What used to be 'SMTP From Address' is now 'Display From Address', with help text reminding admins it must be an address your relay has verified to send for. Second, OSCAR now soft-validates the From: address as you save it: if it looks like a relay-internal authentication identity (ends in @smtp-brevo.com, @smtp.sendgrid.net, etc.) or duplicates the SMTP login exactly, the save still succeeds but a yellow warning surfaces inline, calling out the typical mistake before it silently spam-folders every outgoing email.

A related quality-of-life fix landed in the same release for any administrator who's left a tab open overnight: when an authenticated API call returns 401 (the session cookie expired while the page was idle), OSCAR now detects it everywhere automatically, clears the stale local state, and bounces back to the login page with a clear 'Your session has expired, please sign in again' notice. Replaces the 'every button silently fails on a stale tab' state that previously required a manual hard-reload to recover from.

title: Operational monitoring upgrade — live dashboards, centralised logs, and an automatic watchdog with email alerts
summary: Administrators now have a complete observability stack at their fingertips: a Grafana dashboard with live HTTP, queue and process metrics, a centralised log search across every container (Loki), and — new this release — a self-healing watchdog that auto-restarts the OSCAR server on failure plus an Alertmanager that emails all administrators when something goes wrong (server down, restart loop, queue stuck, sustained run failures, SMTP degraded, login attack burst, memory leak, event-loop lag).
content:
Over the last few releases OSCAR's operations toolkit has been quietly built up to production-grade level. With this release the picture is complete and worth telling end-to-end so administrators know what is now available — and what to expect when something goes wrong.

The new Admin → Admin Dashboard tile group exposes three observability surfaces, all gated by your existing OSCAR administrator login (no separate passwords, no separate provisioning). Grafana shows the OSCAR · Overview dashboard: live HTTP request rate and p95 / p99 latency, Bruno run throughput by status (COMPLETED / FAILED / CANCELLED / TIMEOUT), live queue depth and active-run gauges, authentication and SMTP success/failure rates, plus Node.js process memory, CPU and event-loop lag — refreshed every 15 seconds. Prometheus underneath stores the raw 15-day time series and is reachable directly for ad-hoc PromQL or to confirm scrape-target health. The third tile, Logs (Loki), opens the OSCAR · Logs dashboard: a full live tail of every container's stdout / stderr (OSCAR, Grafana, Prometheus, Watchtower, Bruno workers), a per-container filter, a free-text search box, an errors-only panel, and a log rate timeseries — so triaging an issue no longer requires SSHing into the host and running docker logs by hand.

New this release is the watchdog and alerting layer that ties all of this into actual self-healing operations. Every container that matters now declares a Docker healthcheck — for OSCAR that probe hits the /health endpoint every 30 seconds and confirms the database, the data directory and the worker queue are all responsive. A small autoheal sidecar watches the Docker socket, and if any container fails its healthcheck three times in a row it is automatically restarted — most transient hangs heal themselves within a minute, with no human action required. Above that sits Alertmanager, which receives alerts fired by Prometheus, deduplicates and groups them, and emails every OSCAR administrator using the same SMTP relay you configured on the Server Config tab. Eight alert rules ship by default: OSCAR server unreachable, container restart loop (autoheal can't heal), queue stuck (work present but no run completing), sustained run failure rate above 50 % over 15 minutes, SMTP send failures, login attack burst (over 50 failed logins in 5 minutes), memory above 1 GB for 15 minutes, and event-loop lag above 200 ms. Critical alerts re-page every hour until acknowledged or resolved; warnings repeat every four hours. Each alert carries a runbook annotation pointing to the relevant section of the admin guide, so whoever opens the email knows immediately what to check.

The whole stack is opt-in (enable it on the VPS once with a single docker compose command) and fits in roughly 415 MB of RAM and 600 MB of disk after a month of typical use. Administrators silence alerts during planned maintenance via amtool or the Grafana Silences UI. Detailed setup instructions, the full alert ruleset, and step-by-step verification of the email path are in the Server Admin Guide, sections 13 and 14.

title: Three big quality-of-life features now live: credential redaction, self-service report deletion, and password reset by email
summary: Three improvements that make OSCAR safer to share and easier to use day-to-day. (1) API tokens, client secrets and subscription keys are now automatically redacted from every persisted run report — even on historical runs, which were retroactively scrubbed. (2) Testers and Test Managers can now delete their own reports themselves (with a soft-delete safety net), no longer needing an Administrator. (3) If you forget your password, a self-service 'Forgot password?' link emails you a single-use 24 h reset link.
content:
Three independent improvements have landed across recent releases that, taken together, change how comfortable it feels to use OSCAR in production. We're surfacing them here so administrators and testers know they are available.

First, credential hiding in reports. OSCAR now automatically redacts every credential field from the request and response payloads stored in run reports. Authorization headers, OAuth2 access tokens, client secrets, subscription keys, requestor identifiers, cookies and any other sensitive header are replaced with a [REDACTED — credential] marker before the row is written to the database. The same applies to authentication endpoint bodies, which typically carry client_secret on the way out and access_token on the way back. Crucially, this isn't only forward-looking: a one-shot migration scrubbed every historical run report on the platform, so even reports created before this fix landed are now safe to share with certifiers, auditors or vendor partners. You can open the HTTP Message Chain Viewer on any old run and the credential fields will already be redacted. Anyone who needs to share a report externally can now do so without an extra manual review step.

Second, self-service report deletion for Testers and Test Managers. Until recently, only Administrators could remove a test report — Testers had to wait for an admin to act, which became friction once a single testing campaign produced dozens of runs. The deletion model has been redesigned with a soft-delete safety net: when a Tester or Test Manager deletes one of their own reports, the report disappears immediately from their dashboard and is queued as a deletion request in the Administrator's review panel. The data itself is preserved until an Administrator confirms the deletion, so an accidental click is fully recoverable — Administrators can restore a flagged run with one click. Permanent removal is still strictly an Administrator action, so no one can ever truly destroy a run without explicit administrative confirmation. From the Tester's perspective the workflow now feels normal: delete the noise, keep the dashboard tidy, and trust that nothing is gone for good without admin sign-off.

Third, self-service password reset. A 'Forgot password?' link is now visible on the login page. Enter your email, and OSCAR generates a single-use reset token, stores it with a 24-hour expiry, and emails you a reset link. Click the link, set a new password (subject to the usual policy: minimum 12 characters, at least one uppercase, lowercase and digit), and you're back in — without needing to ask anyone. The flow is rate-limited and uses opaque responses by design, so it can't be used to enumerate which emails have accounts. For Administrators there is also a 'Generate reset link' button on every user's row — useful when SMTP is misconfigured or when an Administrator wants to hand a link to a user out-of-band (Slack, Teams, in person). Both paths share the same single-use token table, so an active link generated either way can be used exactly once.

None of these features changes existing user behaviour by default — they are additions. But they collectively close three of the most frequent operational asks we received across the early months of OSCAR usage.

title: Privacy toggle for Certifiers + Test Managers can now manage their own company users
summary: Two related changes: (1) every company gains a 'Share test reports with Certifiers' toggle on the API Config page — turn it off and Certifiers stop seeing your runs and reports. (2) Test Managers get a new 'Manage Users' menu entry to create, edit, reset passwords for and delete users inside their own company, without needing an Administrator.
content:
Two long-requested capabilities ship together in this release. First, a per-company privacy toggle: open API Config and you'll see a new 'Share test reports with Certifiers' checkbox under the Company API Endpoint card. It defaults to checked — existing companies keep their current behaviour, where Certifiers can see all runs and reports for cross-vendor audit and comparison purposes. Uncheck it and the Certifier role immediately stops seeing your company's data: it disappears from the 'All Reports' listing they use, individual run pages return 'not found' rather than disclosing that the run exists, and the same applies to comparison snapshots. Administrators are unaffected — they always retain full read access regardless of the flag, since they are responsible for the platform itself. Only your company's Test Managers can change the toggle; Testers see it as read-only with an explanatory note, and even Administrators cannot flip it on your behalf — by design the choice belongs to the company that owns the data.

Second, Test Managers gain a new 'Manage Users' menu entry that opens the user-management surface scoped to their own company. They can create new users with role Tester or Test Manager, change a user's role within those two values, reset another user's password, and delete users — all without needing an Administrator to be involved. Cross-company access is blocked at the API level, not just hidden in the UI: even if a Test Manager constructs a request targeting another company's user by ID, the server returns a 'not found' that doesn't disclose existence. Two safety guards prevent self-lockout: a Test Manager cannot delete their own account, and the system refuses to demote or delete the last remaining Test Manager of a company (because then no one would have administrative control over the company's users). The Administrator role and Certifier role remain platform-only and cannot be created or assigned through this new endpoint — those continue to live under the existing Administrator-only management surface.

The combination matters for operators who run real production-grade tests: you can now hand off day-to-day user administration to a designated Test Manager in each company, and you can scope the visibility of in-flight test results to your own organisation while still benefiting from Administrator support. Both features are non-disruptive: nothing about today's behaviour changes for any existing user — Certifier continues to see everything until a Test Manager explicitly opts out, and the new Manage Users menu only appears in the navigation for accounts with the Test Manager role.

title: Offer search criteria — no longer auto-injected on every offer request
summary: A bug was discovered while inspecting actual request payloads in the new HTTP Message Chain Viewer: every offer request was sent with hard-coded default values (currency=EUR, offerMode=INDIVIDUAL, requestedOfferParts=[ADMISSION, RESERVATION]) even when the scenario in the wizard had those fields blank. Per the OSDM specification all of these fields are optional. They are now sent only when the tester explicitly picks them.
content:
Until now, every scenario authored in OSCAR's Test Config wizard ended up sending currency=EUR, offerMode=INDIVIDUAL and requestedOfferParts=[ADMISSION, RESERVATION] on the POST /offers request, regardless of whether the tester had ticked anything in the scenario detail panel. Most testers would never notice — those defaults match the canonical European sale flow most vendors implement — but the new HTTP Message Chain Viewer made the discrepancy visible: the UI showed unchecked boxes and an empty Currency input, yet the actual request body carried the values anyway. That contradicts the OSDM spec, where currency, offerMode, requestedOfferParts, serviceClass, travelClass and flexibilities are all optional offer-search criteria — a compliant client must be free to omit them so the vendor applies its own server-side defaults.

The root cause was a mismatch between OSCAR and the underlying Bruno test collection. OSCAR saved scenarios without an offerSearchCriteria object. The Bruno collection's scenario parser treated that as a 'legacy scenario authored before this object existed' and fell back to hard-coded values to keep very old data files working — exactly the wrong fallback for OSCAR-authored scenarios.

The fix lives entirely in OSCAR (the Bruno collection is unchanged so standalone Bruno users continue to work as before): the Generate & Add Scenario action now writes an offerSearchCriteria object containing only the fields the tester actually picked. An empty object is intentional — it tells Bruno 'the scenario was authored, send only what is explicitly present', producing a request body without those fields. A one-shot migration on data file load also backfills an empty offerSearchCriteria on legacy scenarios that predate this change, so existing scenarios stop emitting the unwanted defaults the moment Test Config is opened. The wizard's initial state also no longer pre-fills hard-coded values — it now reads purely from your Test Framework defaults, so if your framework leaves a field blank, the wizard leaves it blank, and the saved scenario does too.

What changes in practice: a freshly-generated scenario without explicit currency / offerMode / requested offer parts will now produce an offer request body that omits those fields. Vendors apply their own defaults, which is what the spec intends and what certifiers expect to see when reviewing a 'pristine' offer request. If you do want EUR or a specific combination of parts, tick the corresponding pills or type the currency in the scenario detail panel — those choices flow through to the request as they always did. No data files were rewritten on disk; the migration runs in memory and persists the next time you click Save & Apply.

title: HTTP Message Chain Viewer — inspect every request and response, walk the OSDM message chain
summary: Report Builder now stores the full HTTP traffic of every test step (bodies + headers, request and response) and lets you navigate the OSDM exchange — Offer → Booking → Fulfillment → Refund — so you can trace a failing call all the way back to the payload that caused it.
content:
Until now, OSCAR captured assertion outcomes per request but discarded the raw HTTP traffic that produced them. To investigate a non-compliance, certifiers had to re-run the scenario locally with curl or Bruno, which broke the audit trail and was painful for transient failures. With this release, every Bruno step persists its complete request and response — body and headers — into the run database, bounded at 100 KB per body so storage stays under control. Report Builder gains a new 'HTTP Traffic' card you enable by ticking 'Include HTTP request / response bodies + headers' in Step 2 of the wizard. Combine it with the 'Failed only' radio and you land directly on the offending calls.

Click any row and an inline panel opens with a four-tab viewer: Response Body, Request Body, Response Headers, Request Headers. Bodies are rendered as an interactive JSON tree — expand and collapse any nested object, syntax-highlighted keys and values, and a Copy button on every payload that grabs the original raw JSON for paste-into-issue. Headers are rendered as a clean two-column table. Tabs without captured content are greyed out so you immediately see what was recorded.

The chain navigation is the bit that changes the work. OSDM responses don't exist in isolation — a booking references the offer it was built from, a refund references its booking. OSCAR auto-links these via path heuristics (POST /bookings → its parent /offers, /refunds → /refund-offers, etc.) and surfaces them as '← parent' and '→ child' arrows in the viewer header. One click jumps to the linked request and auto-expands it, so you walk the message flow forward and backward without losing your place. Failing booking? Click ← parent and instantly read the offer payload that produced the offerId you're booking against — no more 'I'll need to find that offer in the logs'.

Old runs (made before this release) display empty body tabs because the data wasn't captured at the time — only new runs accumulate the traffic. The bounded body size (100 KB default, MAX_BODY_SIZE env var to tune) covers ~99 % of OSDM payloads while keeping the database growth predictable. Together with the existing pass/fail breakdowns and the vendor capability matrix, the HTTP Traffic viewer turns Report Builder into a self-service investigation tool: certifiers confirm a finding in two clicks, testers reproduce a vendor regression without re-running, and everyone shares the exact same evidence trail.

title: Authentication — paste a token, or let OSCAR fetch one for you (per-tester credentials, five vendor profiles, automatic token caching)
summary: API Config now offers two ways to authenticate against the system under test: paste a pre-fetched Bearer token, or provide your OAuth client credentials directly so OSCAR fetches and refreshes the token for you. Both work; pick whichever fits your test rhythm. Each tester maintains their own credentials.
content:
Until now, the only practical way to run scenarios against an OAuth2-protected OSDM API was to obtain a bearer token outside OSCAR (curl, Postman, your vendor's portal) and paste it into the Profile page. That worked, but tokens expire — typically in an hour — and a tester running back-to-back scenarios spent half their time re-pasting fresh tokens. With this release, the API Config page exposes a second path: tell OSCAR your OAuth credentials once, and the runner fetches a token for you on every run, cached until it expires. Both approaches are first-class — pick whichever matches how your vendor issues credentials.

The new 'Auth Profile' dropdown under OAuth2 mode covers five vendor shapes out of the box: 'Standard OAuth2 — credentials in Basic auth header' (the default, RFC 6749 client_secret_basic, what most compliant servers expect), 'Standard OAuth2 — credentials in body' (RFC 6749 client_secret_post; required by Bileto and Turnit, with an optional Scope field for vendors like Turnit that need scope=retailer-api), 'Paxone — JSON {accountName, accountSecret}' (Paxone's non-OAuth shape with the JSON field names), 'Sqills — custom grant_type URI + Basic + body' (Sqills' extension grant with both username/password in the body and a separate pre-encoded Basic auth header you paste into a new 'Extra Credential' field), and 'Custom — user-supplied request template' (an escape hatch for any vendor not on the list — you provide a JSON template with {{client_id}}, {{client_secret}}, {{scope}}, {{extra}} placeholders, choose JSON or form body, and OSCAR builds the request from your template).

Every tester now maintains their own credentials. Two testers in the same company can use distinct vendor accounts — and one tester saving or rotating their credentials never affects another tester's runs. The 'Company — Shared API Endpoint' card stays for the OSDM URL and the data file (those are genuinely shared); the 'Your Credentials' card below it is yours alone. Existing credentials saved before this release have been migrated to your user account automatically, so you do not have to re-enter anything.

When OSCAR fetches a token for you, it remembers it. The token + its expiry are stored encrypted, and the next run reuses the same token if it still has at least 60 seconds of life left. Back-to-back scenarios no longer hit the vendor's auth endpoint each time. The cache is wiped automatically the moment you change any credential field, so a typo fix is never masked by a stale token. Every run timeline now shows what the runner did: 'Auth — using cached token (expires in 1847s)' on a cache hit, or 'Auth — profile=oauth2_post, scope=retailer-api' followed by 'Auth — token cached until 2026-04-26T15:30:00Z' on a fresh fetch. When a token request fails, the run timeline now surfaces the actual error response from the vendor (e.g. 'invalid_client — Wrong client credentials') instead of just an opaque HTTP status, so you can self-diagnose without server log access. Pre-flight validation on the Run page now lists exactly which credential field is missing — 'OAuth2 client_secret (your credentials)' rather than 'credentials incomplete' — so you fix the right thing on the first try.

title: Booking Flow Actions — opt in to the intermediate steps each scenario should exercise
summary: A new pill selector on every scenario lets testers choose which optional steps of the booking → fulfillment phase to exercise (PATCH passengers, place selection, add/delete ancillary, GET booking). Each selection becomes a row in the Vendor Capability Matrix of the generated report.
content: The OSDM booking flow includes several optional intermediate steps a vendor may or may not implement: patching passenger information between booking and fulfillment, picking specific places on reservable legs, adding or removing ancillary items, or reading the booking back between calls. Until now, these steps either ran unconditionally or were buried behind an all-or-nothing flag in the test harness — testers had no per-scenario control and certifiers couldn't tell from a report which sub-flows the vendor actually supports. With this release, the scenario detail panel gains a new 'Booking Flow Actions' section with five pills: 'PATCH passengers', 'Place selection', 'Add ancillary', 'GET booking' and 'Delete ancillary'. Pills default to unselected for new scenarios — the tester explicitly opts in to each step they want to exercise. Legacy scenarios loaded from pre-existing data files are migrated to all-enabled on load so their historic behaviour is preserved. The section is shown for SALE, REFUND and EXCHANGE scenarios alike (they all start with a booking phase). Under the hood, scenarios now carry a salesFlowActions map that is read by the Bruno test collection through scenarioParser.js; each enabled step is attempted in flow order, and if the offer does not support it (e.g. Add ancillary on an offer with no ancillaryOfferParts) the runner logs NOT_APPLICABLE and continues. Every attempted action becomes one row in the Vendor Capability Matrix at the top of the generated report, so a certifier sees at a glance which booking sub-flows the vendor implements — IMPLEMENTED, PARTIAL, NOT_IMPLEMENTED, ERROR or NOT_APPLICABLE. Only PATCH passengers is wired end-to-end in the Bruno collection at this release; the other four pills emit their flag into the data file and will become active as the library-bruno collection adds the corresponding conditional request scripts. A handful of scenario-editor polish fixes ship alongside: the Action dropdown (PATCH/DELETE) is now hidden for SALE scenarios that have no after-sales action, custom-renamed scenario codes no longer get mislabelled 'Sale' by the code decoder, and a stale reference that produced a misleading 'Network error' on train saves has been removed.

title: Scenario editor overhaul — auto-save, inline rename, per-passenger editor, family grouping, and purchaser linking
summary: The Test Config page has been reworked around silent auto-save, a richer per-passenger editor (with reduction cards and loyalty cards), one-click family grouping for shared last names, and a purchaser-is-a-passenger link — so building a scenario feels closer to filling a form than editing JSON.
content: Auto-save is now the default across the Test Framework: every pill, checkbox, number field, or text input (OSDM version, concurrent session limit, sales flows, transport modes, passenger types, age ranges, IROPS codes, after-sales operations) is persisted 500 ms after the last keystroke or click, with the open/collapse state of sub-sections, the focused input, and the caret position all preserved across the silent re-render. You can rename an existing scenario in place — a new 'Scenario code' field at the top of each scenario's detail panel accepts a new code, normalises it to safe characters, rejects duplicates, and keeps the 'scenarios to run' list in sync automatically. The passenger section has been expanded into a full per-passenger editor: click 'Edit ▾' on any row to unfold a panel with First name, Last name, Date of birth, Email, Phone — plus a free-entry Reduction cards list and a free-entry Loyalty cards list (carrier code + card reference), because reduction and loyalty card codes vary per vendor. The gender selector has been widened to the five OSDM values (MALE, FEMALE, OTHER, UNSPECIFIED, X-legacy); flipping it automatically picks a gender-appropriate first name from the relevant pool — unless you typed a custom name, in which case your value is left alone. A new Family group selector lets you tag multiple passengers as part of one family (badge '👪 F1' in the compact row). Members of the same family share a single last name — editing any member's last name propagates immediately to the others, and joining an existing family adopts its current last name. The Purchaser section gains a 'Purchaser is one of the passengers' checkbox and a passenger picker; when linked, the purchaser fields mirror the chosen passenger's name/email/phone live, and edits to that passenger flow through automatically. When the purchaser is unlinked and empty, OSCAR seeds default values prefixed with 'Purchaser_' so scenario generation never ships an empty purchaser block. Finally, a second Save & Apply button now sits on the same row as 'Create Scenario' at the bottom of the page, so you no longer need to scroll back to the top after editing a long scenario. Several stale-UI bugs in the detail panel have also been fixed: changing Scenario Type (Sale/Refund/Exchange) now correctly shows or hides the Overrule Code field and clears incompatible values, changing Trip Type (SEARCH/SPECIFICATION) reshapes the legs/trip block immediately, and toggling IROPS in the wizard reveals the reason-code dropdown without needing a page refresh.

title: Report Builder — certifier-friendly reports with vendor capability matrix, milestone banners, and collapsible payloads
summary: The Report Builder gains a new Vendor Capability Matrix, explicit scenario milestone banners in the log stream, collapsible JSON dumps for 'Selected Offer'-style output, per-endpoint context tags (refund mode, flexibility, passenger count), and a handful of correctness fixes — so a certifier can read conformance results without line-by-line log diving.
content: The top of every generated report now shows a Vendor Capability Matrix: one row per endpoint, in Bruno's execution order (Access Token → System Infos → Common Requests → Refund → Exchange), each labelled IMPLEMENTED, PARTIAL, NOT_IMPLEMENTED, or ERROR. A 501 response or a 404 on a spec-defined endpoint is automatically classified as NOT_IMPLEMENTED; a 5xx other than 501 is an ERROR; 2xx with every assertion passing is IMPLEMENTED; 2xx with some assertions failing is PARTIAL. Each row carries inline context chips extracted from the request body: refund and exchange endpoints show 'mode: reason-code (overruleCode=ILLNESS)' or 'mode: voluntary', offer requests show 'flexibility' and 'paxCount', bookings show 'paxCount' and 'currency' — so a certifier can tell why a refund succeeded on a non-refundable offer without opening the raw payload. In the execution log, scenario boundaries are now emitted as explicit milestone events: 'Scenario start', 'Retry (attempt N/M)', 'Scenario skipped', 'Scenario end', each rendered as a colour-coded full-width banner. Every log row is stamped with its current scenario and attempt index, so the header never lies about which scenario's output you are looking at. When a Bruno script dumps a large object to the console ('Selected Offer', offer JSON, etc.), consecutive continuation lines are now coalesced into a single collapsible pill — click 'selectedOffer  9 lines' to expand the full JSON in place. Failed assertions render their error message on a dedicated wrapping line beneath the assertion name (previously truncated to 180 px / 60 characters). Three correctness fixes land in the same release: assertion durations are now correct (Bruno reports runDuration in seconds; the extractor was treating it as milliseconds, so a 2.8 s request appeared as '3 ms'), the assertion classifier no longer cross-routes offer fields like 'exchangeable' or 'refundable' into the exchange/refund domains (word-boundary match), and the capability matrix is ordered by execution sequence rather than by status severity — matching certifiers' top-to-bottom reading mental model.

title: Structured test reports — filter, sort, and analyse assertion results by category
summary: OSCAR now stores every test assertion with rich metadata (category, OSDM domain, severity) and provides powerful filtering tools to focus on exactly the results you need.
content: Test results are no longer just pass/fail counts in an HTML report. Every assertion from every Bruno test run is now automatically classified and stored in the database with structured metadata: 11 assertion categories (HTTP status, business logic, data consistency, field validation, and more), 8 OSDM domains (offer, booking, fulfillment, refund, exchange, passenger, system, infrastructure), 4 severity levels (critical, major, minor, info), and offer part types (admission, reservation, ancillary). When you open a completed run's detail page, a new Assertions section displays all results in a three-level hierarchy: test suites, then HTTP requests, then individual assertions. Filter buttons let you instantly switch between All, Passed, or Failed assertions. Dropdown filters for Category and Domain let you focus on specific areas — for example, show only 'business_logic' assertions in the 'booking' domain to see exactly which booking validations are failing. Each assertion shows its category badge (blue), domain badge (purple), and severity badge (colour-coded from green to red). The execution log also gains new filtering controls: filter by level (stdout, stderr, info, error), search by keyword, and copy or download filtered logs with one click. For Certifiers and Administrators, a new Report Builder page provides a full report generation workflow: select one or more completed runs, configure filters (categories, domains, severity levels, pass/fail status), and generate a structured conformance report with summary statistics, domain and category breakdowns, and the complete filtered assertion list. Reports can be exported as CSV for analysis in spreadsheets, or printed directly from the browser. Certifiers can save their filter configurations as reusable templates, making it easy to generate consistent reports across multiple test campaigns.

title: New role: Test Manager — governance for multi-user companies
summary: A new Test Manager role gives designated users exclusive control over the test framework, test data, and shared scenarios, while regular Testers focus on running tests.
content: OSCAR now supports a Test Manager role at the company level, designed for organisations where multiple testers share the same API environment. The Test Manager is the only person who can configure the Test Framework (Section 1: OSDM version, sales flows, transport modes, passenger types) and the Test Data (Section 2: train resources with routes, schedules, and service configurations). Regular Testers can view these configurations but cannot modify them — the sections appear in read-only mode with a clear banner indicating they are managed by the Test Manager. The Test Manager can also create shared scenarios that all Testers in the company can use in their test runs. Shared scenarios are marked with a purple lock badge and cannot be modified or deleted by Testers. However, Testers can duplicate any shared scenario to create their own personal copy, which they can then customise freely. Testers retain full control over their own scenarios: they can create new ones, edit them, delete them, and include any mix of shared and personal scenarios in their test runs. This separation ensures that the core test configuration remains stable and consistent across the team, while individual Testers have the flexibility to experiment with their own scenario variations. Administrators create Test Manager accounts from the Admin panel by selecting the 'Test Manager' role and assigning them to the appropriate company.

title: Scenario passenger list management — add, remove, and change passenger types
summary: Testers can now modify the passenger list of any scenario directly from the scenario detail view, without recreating the scenario from scratch.
content: Previously, the number and type of passengers in a scenario could only be defined during scenario creation in the wizard. If you needed to test with a different passenger mix — say, adding a child to an adults-only scenario or removing a passenger to simplify debugging — you had to delete the scenario and recreate it from the wizard. With this update, each scenario's Passenger section now shows a compact, category-based view of all passengers. Each passenger displays its category (Adult, Child, Youth, Senior, etc.) in a dropdown that can be changed at any time — changing the category automatically regenerates the appropriate date of birth based on the age range for that type. A new 'Add Passenger' button at the bottom of the list lets you add passengers of any category with a single click — the name, email, phone number, and date of birth are auto-generated with realistic random data. Each passenger also has a 'Remove' button to shrink the list (you cannot remove the last remaining passenger). All changes are reflected immediately and saved when you click 'Save & Apply'. Shared scenarios managed by a Test Manager remain read-only for Testers — passenger modifications are only allowed on scenarios you own.

title: Concurrent scenario execution — run multiple scenarios in parallel
summary: OSCAR now supports parallel execution of test scenarios, controlled by a per-company concurrent session limit, with a live queue status panel showing all running and waiting jobs.
content: For companies testing against APIs that can handle multiple simultaneous requests, OSCAR now offers a parallel execution mode. Instead of running all scenarios one after another in a single long session, each scenario can run as an independent process — dramatically reducing total test time. The concurrent session limit is configured per company in the Test Framework settings (Section 1), with a default of 1 (sequential, same as before) and a maximum of 10. When you launch a run in parallel mode, OSCAR creates a separate job for each scenario in your scenariosToRun list, groups them in a batch, and feeds them to the queue. The queue respects the concurrent session limit: if your company allows 3 parallel sessions and you submit 7 scenarios, the first 3 start immediately while the remaining 4 wait in the queue. As each scenario completes, the next one starts automatically. Jobs are never refused — they simply wait for a free slot. The New Run page now shows a live Company Queue panel that updates every 5 seconds, displaying all running and queued jobs for your company with their scenario name, user, and position in the queue. Your own jobs are highlighted with a 'you' badge. The Dashboard groups parallel runs into collapsible batches, showing the batch date, scenario count, and completion progress at a glance — click to expand and see individual scenario results. On the server side (Linux only), each parallel run executes in its own isolated workspace using symlinks to the shared test collection, ensuring no file collisions between concurrent Bruno processes. A configurable stagger delay (default 2 seconds) between launches prevents overwhelming the provider API with simultaneous requests.

title: Dynamic scenario management — configure your test runs directly from OSCAR
summary: Testers can now select which scenarios to run and edit scenario parameters directly from the OSCAR web interface, without touching the data file manually.
content: OSCAR now includes a dedicated Test Config page that gives testers full control over their test campaigns from within the web interface. Previously, configuring a test run required manually editing a JSON data file and re-uploading it — a process that was error-prone and time-consuming. With this release, testers can simply open the Test Config page, tick the scenarios they want to include in their next run, and edit any scenario parameter directly in the browser: scenario type (Sale, Refund, Exchange), OSDM version, desired flexibility, overrule code, trip origin and destination, passenger details, offer search criteria, and fulfillment options are all editable inline. The selection and changes are saved back to the server with a single click of the 'Save & Apply' button, which also verifies that the changes were correctly persisted before confirming. The New Run page now shows a live summary of how many scenarios are queued, so testers always know exactly what will execute before clicking Start. The Test Config page also supports uploading an existing data file or starting from scratch, and includes a Delete option to reset the configuration entirely. The next planned step is to go further and allow the creation of brand new scenarios directly from the OSCAR web interface — enabling testers to build their entire test configuration from scratch without any JSON editing.

title: Improved report deletion — Testers request, Administrators decide
summary: The deletion process has been redesigned to give Testers a safe soft-delete workflow while keeping permanent data removal exclusively in the hands of Administrators.
content: OSCAR now enforces a clear two-step deletion lifecycle for test reports. When a Tester removes a report from their dashboard, it is no longer deleted immediately — instead it is marked as a deletion request and forwarded to the Administrator queue. The run disappears from the Tester's view straight away, but the data is fully preserved until an Administrator reviews and confirms the action. Administrators gain a dedicated 'Pending Deletion Requests' panel in the All Reports tab, where they can confirm each request to permanently remove the data, or restore it to make it visible again if the deletion was accidental. Administrators can also independently flag any run for deletion from the main runs list — flagged runs remain visible to Testers with a clear 'Flagged by Admin' warning badge, so nothing disappears without the Tester being aware. Permanent deletion is exclusively an administrator privilege and is always a deliberate, confirmed action.

title: Security hardening and multi-scenario runs now available
summary: Session security has been tightened and testers can now run multiple scenarios in a single submission using the scenariosToRun parameter in the data file.
content: Two significant improvements have been shipped in this release. On the security front, OSCAR now generates a fresh JWT secret every time the server starts, which means all active web sessions are automatically invalidated on restart — users must sign in again after a server reboot. Your API credentials (endpoint URL, bearer token, OAuth2 client ID and secret) are unaffected and remain safely encrypted in the database across restarts. Additionally, OSCAR now detects authentication failures during test execution and displays a clear warning banner on the run detail page, distinguishing between a malformed token (YAML format error) and an expired or revoked token (HTTP 401), so testers know exactly what to fix. On the execution side, multi-scenario runs are now fully supported: add a scenariosToRun array to your data file listing the scenario codes you want to execute, and OSCAR will run them all in sequence in a single submission. If a particular route has no inventory, the runner retries up to three times before skipping to the next scenario — preventing a missing offer from blocking your entire test session.

title: Welcome to OSCAR — the OSDM Conformance Automation Runner is born
summary: The OSDM community now has a dedicated platform for running conformance tests against OSDM-compliant APIs.
content: OSCAR (OSDM Conformance Automation Runner) is a new platform created by UIC to help rail operators and distributors verify that their OSDM API implementations meet the official specification. By submitting your API endpoint and credentials, OSCAR automatically executes the full OTST test suite using Bruno and produces detailed conformance reports — all without requiring any local toolchain setup. Whether you are a system integrator preparing for certification or an operator continuously monitoring conformance across software releases, OSCAR gives you a repeatable, auditable, and centrally managed testing workflow backed by the authority of UIC.
